reasoning: Successful kinetic ASAT intercepts (interceptor hitting a satellite) are rare; since the Dec 2022 baseline only a small number of confirmed successful tests have occurred, and the US holds a destructive-test moratorium. China/Russia/India could each add one, so a median of ~2 with a fat low tail and modest upside fits.

Baseline was 8 in 2022 (ISS, Tianhe, plus docked capsules); by 2030 the ISS likely still flies (~4), Tiangong is expanded, multiple crewed capsules are typically docked, and commercial stations (Axiom, Starlab, Orbital Reef) plus possible Starship add upside, but ISS retirement risk caps the low side.

No confirmed deliberate offensive ASAT use against a satellite itself has occurred despite years of conflict; ongoing jamming/dazzling typically targets ground links or users rather than the satellite, and kinetic/co-orbital offensive use remains a high-escalation rarity, so a low-moderate probability is warranted.

Far from repeal, the Wolf Amendment is gaining momentum toward permanent codification (2025 Frank Wolf Space Security Act) amid hawkish US-China space tensions; overturning legislation before 2030 is very unlikely, so status-quo YES is near-certain.
